1. The animation shows how inflation wears down the buying power of a fixed income. Three illustrative retirees each get the same raise of 2% a year. Edna retired in Jan 1949, Ruth in Aug 2006, and Carl in Jan 1966. Each person has a row of crates, which stands for what their income can buy.

2. The rows start at about the same length in frames 1 and 2. Then they shrink at different rates as the years pass, and the right-hand end of each row goes dark. By year 20 (frames 3 to 6), Edna's row is still full, Ruth's is slightly shortened, and Carl's is mostly dark. The labels read 10 crates for Edna, about 9 for Ruth and about 4 for Carl.

3. The same 2% raise protects buying power well or badly depending on how fast prices actually rose over those 20 years. In Edna's period, prices rose slowly enough that her raise kept up. In Carl's period, from 1966, prices rose much faster than 2% a year, so his income bought less than half as much by year 20. The label "US only · history, not a forecast" tells the viewer the past periods are examples and don't predict what will happen next.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that a payout that rises by a fixed 2% a year can lose a lot of purchasing power if inflation runs high. In my role as a 64-year-old comparing two payout options, I would want to check whether either option adjusts with inflation and how it would hold up in a high-inflation stretch.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the three examples and the "history, not a forecast" caveat. It doesn't mention annuities or tell the viewer to choose anything.
